deep.reconstruction:
This page is from Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, published by Dedekind 1867). It is the end of §2 and the start of §3 of the historical part.

(a) Last line of §2. Cauchy's route to the convergence of the Fourier series works if one assumes the following. For a given periodic f there is a function φ(x+iy) that is finite for y>0 and whose real part at y=0 equals f(x). Conversely, this existence statement can be derived from the Fourier series. In modern terms: if f has Fourier series Σ(a_n cos nx + b_n sin nx), take φ(z) = a_0/2 + Σ (a_n − i b_n) e^{inz}. For y>0 this is a power series in q = e^{iz} with |q| = e^{−y} < 1. Its real part tends to f as y→0+. This is the Abel/Poisson-summation and harmonic-extension viewpoint.

(b) §3 history. In January 1829 Dirichlet (Crelle's Journal Bd. IV, p. 157) settled representability rigorously. His class was functions that are integrable throughout and have only finitely many maxima and minima.

(c) The key mathematical content: two classes of convergent series. Let Σu_k be a convergent series.
- Class 1: Σ|u_k| converges (modern: absolute convergence).
- Class 2: Σ|u_k| diverges (modern: conditional convergence).
- Claim: class-1 series can be rearranged arbitrarily without changing the sum. The value of a class-2 series depends on the order of its terms.

Argument for class 2, step by step:
1. Let a_1, a_2, ... be the positive terms in order, and −b_1, −b_2, ... the negative terms.
2. Then Σa = Σb = ∞. Proof by cases:
   - If both were finite, Σ|u_k| = Σa + Σb < ∞, so the series would be class 1.
   - If exactly one were infinite, the partial sums would tend to ±∞, so the series would diverge, contradicting convergence.
3. 'Obviously' a suitable reordering then gives any prescribed value C. The construction continues on the next page:
   - take positive terms until the partial sum exceeds C, then negative terms until it falls below C, and repeat;
   - the deviation from C is bounded by the term just before the last sign change;
   - since a_n, b_n → 0 (implicit: the terms of a convergent series tend to 0), the deviation → 0.
   This is the Riemann rearrangement (series) theorem.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The case analysis showing Σa = Σb = ∞ is complete and correct, given that the series is assumed convergent.

Implicit step (the proof is completed on the next page): the rearrangement argument needs a_n → 0 and b_n → 0, which follows from convergence of the original series. It also needs the two divergent sums so that each crossing of C is always possible.
The statement that class-1 series may be rearranged freely is asserted without proof here. It is standard and true (Dirichlet 1837 / Cauchy).

results.what: Classification of convergent series into those that stay convergent when all signs are made positive and those that do not. Order-independence of the sum holds for the former.
results.modern_name: Absolute vs. conditional convergence; unconditional summability of absolutely convergent series
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy (1821, Cours d'analyse) for absolute convergence tests; Dirichlet (1837) for the observation that the sum of non-absolutely convergent series depends on order

results.what: For a conditionally convergent real series, both the positive part and the negative part diverge, so a rearrangement can converge to any prescribed C. Greedy construction completed on the next page.
Remark that Cauchy's 1826 proof works if one assumes a function φ(x+iy) bounded for y>0 whose real part at y=0 is f. Conversely, this follows from the Fourier series.
results.modern_name: Harmonic / holomorphic extension to the upper half-plane; Abel–Poisson summation of Fourier series
results.usually_credited_to: Poisson (Poisson kernel), Cauchy; the remark itself is in Riemann's published Habilitationsschrift

deep.surprise_reason: This is a fair copy of the well-known published text of Riemann's 1854 Habilitationsschrift (§3). The rearrangement theorem here is famous and universally credited to Riemann from exactly this source.

checkable.asserts: The alternating harmonic series (conditionally convergent) sums to log 2; the expression should simplify to 0.
The positive part of the alternating harmonic series diverges (should be False), illustrating that Σa = ∞.
The negative part also diverges (should be False), illustrating that Σb = ∞.
Rearranging as two positive terms then one negative term changes the sum to (3/2)log 2; the expression should be 0. This shows order-dependence for class-2 series.
Example of a class-1 (absolutely convergent) series (should be True), whose sum is order-independent.
